# Traceability

Traces every requirement from design through to a passing test and the release it
shipped in. Part of the Definition of Done in `CLAUDE.md`.

The roadmap (§37) provides a **family-level** baseline proving every requirement
family has an implementation route. **Stage 2 expands this to one row per
individual requirement** (`M##-FR-##`, `D##-FR-##`, `SEC-##`, `PRV-##`, `AI-NFR-##`,
`MG-##`, etc.) with design, code, automated-test and release references. No
requirement may reach **Done** without a complete individual row.

## Family-level baseline (roadmap §37)

**The Status column is derived from the requirement rows below it, never asserted here.** This table
sat at *"Not started"* on all twelve families through nineteen stages of work, because the
integrity guardrail matched only rows beginning `| M##-FR-## |` and never saw these. It is now
checked: `tests/guardrails/traceability-integrity.test.ts` recomputes each family from its own
requirement rows and fails if a family claims anything else.

| POS service · API-05 (§31.1, hard rules #1/#2/#10, P-08, M12–M15) | `services/pos/` (`sale-intake`, `index`) | **The server does not get to say no.** By the time a sale reaches this endpoint it has already happened — the till committed locally (#1), the money is in the drawer, the receipt is printed, the customer has gone. A server that refuses a sale it dislikes and a till that treats refusal as *"drop it"* together delete a sale that really happened while the cash for it sits in the drawer, and the day will not balance with the evidence thrown away by both systems that had it. So **a well-formed sale is always banked and everything wrong with it becomes a visible exception attached to it** (#10, P-08); `banked` is typed as the literal `true`, and the reply is **202, never 4xx**. The only refusal is a payload that cannot be *read* as a sale, and it tells the lane to keep it rather than discard it. **The server never corrects a sale to make it valid** — the customer paid what the till charged, and rewriting it to the catalogue price makes the books agree with the catalogue and disagree with reality (#2, proven by scanning the module's exports). Findings are ranked by how fast a person must act rather than by value: **a recalled product sold outranks every number on the list**, because it is in a customer's hands, and the lane is not blamed for it (its pack predated the block). A price difference from a lane that was behind is *informational* — pricing from the pack it holds is exactly what a lane is supposed to do offline — and *material* only when the lane was current. Late is not wrong; a clock ahead of the server is. Informational findings are **counted, not listed**, because forty explained differences from one lane back off a long weekend bury the one that is not explained. Tested in `tests/unit/service-pos.test.ts` |
| **Thirteen APIs, one surface** (§30, SEC-03, §31.1) | `tests/integration/thirteen-apis-one-surface.test.ts` | The questions that only exist once all thirteen are assembled and that no single service's tests can reach: every API in the catalogue is actually served and none is invented; no two services claim one address; **every write on the whole surface is idempotent**, because the till, the handheld and the driver's phone all resend what they could not confirm; every path is versioned and every route declares a permission; and **each permission is spelled one way across every service** — `pos.sale.read` against `pos.sales.read` both look right in review and one of them guards an endpoint with a permission nobody holds, so case, separator *and plural* are normalised away, with a tripwire proving the normalisation catches the near-miss. The API catalogue is **read from `docs/api/catalogue.md`** rather than restated, so the two cannot drift. 12 assertions |
| Catalogue service · API-02 (§31, M03/M05, §28, M10-FR-04, P-01, P-08) | `services/catalogue/` (`pack`, `index`) | The first domain service on the kernel, and **the file the shop trades on when the internet is down**. A bad read shows one person a wrong answer; a bad **pack** installs on every lane and is the only truth any of them has — and the lane cannot ring anybody about it, because not being able to is why it holds a pack. Refused before anything is signed: **a pack much smaller than the shop** (the truncated-export failure pointed outward, and worse — it is internally consistent, signs, installs, and the first to notice is a customer whose item will not scan; a real discontinuation is **acknowledged by count**, and an acknowledgement that does not match what left is refused as a rubber stamp); a version that does not move forward (a price rollback nobody performed); prices approved by whoever drafted them (§28 surviving the step that reaches the shelf edge); a product with no tax class (OC-21); a price above MRP (a lane would charge it offline all week with nobody able to stop it). On the lane: **a pack that fails its signature is rejected and the shop keeps trading on the last one it trusted** — `shopKeepsTrading: true`, never a blank catalogue, never a stopped till, and never silently (staleness is shown in days). HMAC-SHA256 with `timingSafeEqual`; the signing key comes from the environment (#4). Found by building it: the kernel's card-data guard fired on **EAN-13 barcodes**, whose check digit is computed the same alternating way Luhn is — see the kernel row. Tested in `tests/unit/service-catalogue.test.ts` |
| Service kernel (§30 conventions, §31.1, §27.1, SEC-02/03/07/12, OB-01) | `services/kernel/` (`errors`, `router`, `pipeline`) | The foundation all thirteen APIs sit on, so no cross-cutting rule is written thirteen times and correct twelve. **Every convention is enforced at route REGISTRATION, not at request time** — a service serving an unversioned path, a write with no idempotency, or an endpoint with no permission **fails to start**, rather than failing on the one request in a thousand that exercises the gap; `buildRouter` names every malformed route at once. **The three-part error (§27.1) cannot be constructed incomplete** — and the part every API omits, *whether the data was saved*, has no default, with `unknown` a legitimate answer for a timeout, because answering "failed" when the truth is unknown is what takes the money twice. **Two guards run on the way OUT and refuse rather than redact:** a reply carrying another tenant's id is not sent (the backstop for the one query that was not scoped), and a reply carrying something structurally a card number is not sent (hard rule #3) — Luhn-checked **plus an issuer prefix plus a card-length check**, because Luhn alone was not enough: EAN-13's check digit is computed the same alternating way, so about **one barcode in ten passes Luhn by chance** — the first version of the guard blocked a catalogue pack, the single most important response in the system. Lengths 13 and 14 are excluded deliberately (EAN-13, ITF-14), which costs a legacy 13-digit Visa and buys a guard quiet enough to leave switched on. A different request under a used `Idempotency-Key` is **refused, never answered with the stored result** — a sale of 400 under the key of a sale of 250 would otherwise report success and bank 250. Found and fixed while building: the audit fired only on the success path, so a **refused** write left no trace, which is the event an audit trail exists for. Tested in `tests/unit/service-kernel.test.ts` |

| Store edge (P-01, #1, NFR-03, §31) | `edge/store-edge/` (`durability`, `index`) | **The receipt prints after the durable write, never before.** The other order produces the worst failure the product has: a sale the cashier saw succeed, the customer paid for and walked away from, which was never written anywhere — nobody finds out, the day is short, and the till is blamed for a counting error that never happened. It is also **the one place in the product where refusing a sale is correct**, and the reason is the moment: the edge refuses *before* the sale completes (nothing has happened, the customer is still standing there), while `services/pos` refuses *after* (the money is in the drawer and they have gone). Same word, opposite consequences. When the disk fills, `SHED_ORDER` decides what is given up — telemetry, prefetched catalogue, synced history, then pending movements, which a recount can rebuild — and **an unsynced sale is last, with nothing permitted after it**; `shedsAnySale` is typed as the literal `false`, and where shedding everything else is not enough the lane refuses new sales rather than deleting money already taken. Health is reported in **hours behind and hours of headroom**, not items pending, because "247 items" is a number staff learn to ignore. Tested in `tests/unit/store-edge.test.ts` |
| API client (§30, §31.1, §27.1, P-01, P-08) | `packages/api-client/` | **The idempotency key is minted when the person acts, not when the request is sent** — the reason this package exists. Generate it per attempt and a retry carries a new one, so a till resending a sale it could not confirm creates a second sale, and the server doing everything right banks both. Every server-side guarantee is undone by a client that gets this wrong, and it is wrong by default in almost every HTTP client, because retrying is a transport concern and the key looks like a transport detail. An `Intent` is created once and carries its key through every attempt, reconnection and restart — proved by a test that restarts the application and checks the key survived. **`wasItSaved` reaches the person** in words rather than being flattened to "request failed". Offline writes queue and say nothing is lost (P-01); a decided refusal is *not* retried, because resending it forever buries everything behind it; the queue drains oldest-first, since a refund arriving before its sale reaches a server that has never heard of the sale. Reads fall back to cache **with their age in the answer**, telling the reader to stop deciding on figures once they are hours old. Tested in `tests/unit/api-client.test.ts` |
| Persistence adapters (hard rule #2, M08, §29, OB-01) | `services/api/src/adapters.ts` | Until these, the API booted, answered and **forgot everything** — every service was wired to a stub. **Everything is an event**: there is no products table, no sales table, no stock table and no "current pack" column. A sale is `SaleCommitted`, a movement is `InventoryMoved`, a published price list is `CataloguePublished`, and every balance and every *current* anything is **projected by reading the stream forward**. That is not taste — it is the only shape in which hard rule #2 can hold, because a table with an `UPDATE` on it is a quantity somebody can overwrite and no discipline in the application layer survives one hurried fix. A test asserts no mutable `sales`, `products`, `stock` or `inventory` table exists. Sale dedupe is keyed on the **sale's own id**, so a till resending collapses to one even under a different transport key. Proved end to end in `tests/integration/it-remembers.test.ts` against real PostgreSQL: publish a pack, sell against it, resend twice, project stock from out-of-order movements, and watch the database refuse an `UPDATE`. Three faults found by running it — an append that **deduped against a previous test run's pack** (the store right, the test wrong, now run-scoped), a query string put in the path instead of the query field, and a fixture dated ahead of the real clock which `committed_in_the_future` caught doing its job |
| Atomic multi-event append (audit FND-01 / GAP-DATA-01, hard rule #2, §30.2) | `packages/persistence/src/event-store.ts` (`appendBatch`), `packages/persistence/src/sql-client.ts` (`transaction`), `packages/persistence/src/pg-client.ts` (`pgPoolClient`), `services/api/src/adapters.ts` (`bankSale`, `recordReturn`), `services/api/src/main.ts` | A money-critical command writes **more than one event** — a banked sale plus its receipt-number index, a return plus its tenant-wide reporting projection — and before this they were two separate appends, so a crash between them left a **partial set**: a sale with no receipt, a report missing a return. The database's own answer to "all of them, or none" is a transaction, and the store had no way to open one — the `SqlClient` port was `query()` only (audit GAP-DATA-01). This adds an OPTIONAL `transaction<T>(fn)` to the port (the callback's reads run on the SAME pinned connection, so they see the batch's own uncommitted writes — the subtle correctness point, tested), implemented over a real `pg.Pool` by a new `pgPoolClient` (BEGIN → run → COMMIT, ROLLBACK-and-rethrow on any throw, connection always released — `pgClient` stays query-only so the many single-write stores and the integration harness's `pg.Client` are untouched). On top of it, `EventStore.appendBatch` commits a whole set atomically: the SQL store wraps a batch of two-or-more in one transaction (a lone append needs none — a single INSERT is atomic, so the common path pays no BEGIN/COMMIT), the in-memory reference stages then applies in one pass; each event keeps its own idempotency key so a whole-batch resend dedups every event and the results line up one-to-one. `bankSale` and `recordReturn` now use it; `services/api/src/main.ts` gives the production event store the transactional adapter. **Proved against real PostgreSQL** in `tests/integration/appends-are-atomic.test.ts`: a good batch commits both events; a batch whose second event violates `event_ledger_id_uq` mid-flight rolls the first one back too, leaving the stream empty and neither key resolvable — a crash mid-command leaves *nothing*. Plus the store contract (`tests/unit/persistence-event-store.test.ts` — batch order/seq, whole-batch replay dedup, cross-stream, in-batch duplicate collapse, and a transactional fake proving rollback + tx-scoped read-back) and the connector envelope (`tests/unit/persistence-pg-connector.test.ts` — BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK/release, pinned connection). **HONEST SCOPE:** this draws the atomic boundary and wires the two money-critical sites; the other ~90 single-append call sites are already atomic on their own and were not touched |
| Tamper-evident audit chain (audit FND-02 / GAP-SEC-03, SEC-07, M34-FR-01, hard rule #6, §35) | `services/kernel/src/audit-chain.ts`, `services/kernel/src/audit-sink.ts`, `db/migrations/0010_audit_log_hash_chain.sql`, `scripts/verify-audit-chain.mts`, `services/api/src/main.ts` | The kernel writes an `audit_log` row for every write and every refusal — who did what, when, and what they were told, including "no". The rows were **append-only at the database** (0004/0008 refuse UPDATE and DELETE) but **unsealed**: nothing bound a row to the one before it, so a row inserted, removed or reordered *behind* the database — a restored backup with a line quietly dropped, a direct write by whoever holds the credentials — left no trace. Append-only stops edits **through the application**; it does not make an out-of-band change **detectable**. Now each row carries the **SHA-256 hash of its predecessor within the same tenant** (§35) and a hash over its own sealed contents — actor, path, outcome status, and the **timestamp** (sealed as a writer-supplied ISO string, not the DB's `now()`, precisely so a back-dated row breaks the seal). Change one byte of one row, or drop one, and `verifyAuditChain` names the exact row where the chain breaks (P-08 — tamper-EVIDENT, not tamper-proof). The seal is computed once in `services/kernel/src/audit-chain.ts` and used by BOTH the writer (`SqlAuditSink`) and the verify tool, so the two cannot drift. SHA-256 (real cryptographic digest via `node:crypto`), not the pure-TypeScript FNV-1a that `packages/audit` carries as its dependency-free default. Writes seal under a **per-tenant advisory lock inside one transaction** (built on FND-01's `pgPoolClient`), so two concurrent audit writes cannot fork the chain; a **unique index on `(tenant_id, prev_hash)`** is the belt-and-suspenders fork guard — even a bug cannot silently branch a chain, it fails loudly. The migration is additive and idempotent (two nullable columns + the index; pre-migration rows are an unsealed prefix the verifier skips). Ships a runnable verifier (`pnpm verify:audit`) that exits non-zero on any break, for CI/cron/an auditor's terminal. Proved against **real PostgreSQL** (`tests/integration/the-trail-is-kept.test.ts`): rows written through the real sink link genesis→…→n, the whole chain verifies, a hand-crafted forked row is refused by the database, and edit/delete are still refused. The verifier's tamper-detection (edited row, removed row, forged row, per-tenant isolation) is pinned in `tests/unit/audit-chain.test.ts`. **HONEST SCOPE:** this seals the production kernel `audit_log` (the request-level access trail). The richer domain-state audit in `packages/audit` (before/after reconstruction) is a separate, currently-unwired trail whose `Hasher` port already accepts SHA-256 |
| Rate limiting + auth-attempt lockout (audit FND-03 / GAP-SEC-04, SEC-03, §30) | `services/kernel/src/rate-limit.ts`, `services/kernel/src/pipeline.ts`, `services/kernel/src/errors.ts`, `services/kernel/src/http-server.ts`, `services/api/src/main.ts` | The kernel had exactly ONE 429 in the whole product — the AI budget gate — so nothing capped how fast a caller could hammer the API, and nothing slowed a script guessing tokens against the sign-in path (audit GAP-SEC-04). Two protections, kept apart because they answer different threats. **Rate limiting** smooths VOLUME: a token bucket per key refills at a sustained rate and allows a burst to a capacity; over-rate calls are refused 429 with a **`Retry-After`** so a retry is paced, not a hot loop. The pipeline checks it **per source IP BEFORE authentication** (a flood — including of the sign-in path — is capped whether or not it ever presents a valid token) and **per tenant AFTER** (one tenant's burst cannot starve another's lane, §35, keyed on the signed tenant never anything the caller sent). **Auth-attempt lockout** stops GUESSING: consecutive failed sign-ins from one source trip an **exponential backoff** — below a threshold nothing locks (a mistyped password is not an attack), at and beyond it the source is locked for `base·2^(n)` seconds capped at a max, and a locked source is refused 429 WITHOUT the token even being examined, so a brute-force run slows to the backoff's pace; a **single success clears the count**. The source IP is set by the HTTP server from the leftmost `x-forwarded-for` (the ingress sets it) or the socket peer. Both are PORTS (`RateLimiter`, `AuthThrottle`) with in-process token-bucket / backoff implementations — real components, not test doubles (ephemeral state is correct here, the way `RequestMetrics` counters are), driven by an injected clock so a test proves the refusal AND the recovery with no waiting. The 429 carries a complete three-part error (§27.1); `ApiError` gained an optional `retryAfterSeconds` the pipeline surfaces as the header. Tested in `tests/unit/rate-limit.test.ts` (token-bucket burst/refill/per-key isolation/cap; backoff below-threshold/lock/doubling-capped/success-clears/source-isolation) and `tests/unit/service-kernel.test.ts` (the pipeline returns 429 + Retry-After on a per-IP flood, isolates sources, locks a source then refuses even a valid token, and lets a genuine sign-in clear the count). **HONEST SCOPE:** the in-process limiter is correct for the single-store box and a single API instance; a MULTI-INSTANCE cloud swaps the port for a shared Redis-backed limiter (technology baseline) so the limit is global and a lockout cannot be evaded by hitting another pod — the same port / deployment-adapter split as idempotency, and the follow-on for horizontal scale |
| Customer "delete my data" — the DPO erasure console, browser-verified (Item 5 slice 5d, completes Item 5, owner decision — DEVELOPMENT-APPROVED, LEGAL CONFIRMATION REQUIRED) (M20-FR-04 / PRV / DPDP, §28, P-04, P-07, P-08, hard rules #6 #10) | `apps/web-erp/web/erasure-console.html`, `apps/web-erp/web/erasure-console.js`, `tests/e2e/erasure-console.e2e.ts` | The last piece a unit/integration test cannot prove: that a data-protection officer at the actual SCREEN carries out a verified erasure under the two-person rule. A genuine **thin client** (no erasure logic, no money maths) shows the located PII for a verified request and drives the control — a **checker** approves, then a **different maker** executes; the backend runs the production `@sre/customer` engines (plan / authorise / execute / tombstone / prevent-restore). It renders the outcome **honestly**: which categories were deleted, which kept-but-anonymised, and which the law keeps in full — with a **legal-confirmation-required** banner on the page so the screen never implies compliance. Bilingual EN/TA, 44px targets, `aria-live` status, both colour themes. **Browser-verified end to end** (`tests/e2e/erasure-console.e2e.ts`, real Chromium against a Node backend running the same engines over an in-memory simulated holding — no erasure maths in the browser): the located PII is shown; an execution with **no second approver** is refused; the **same officer** approving and executing is refused (SoD §28); a **different maker** completes it, the tombstone showing the marketing profile **erased**, the audit record **minimised**, the tax invoice **retained and untouched** (#6); and a later re-import of the erased person's data is **refused** (prevent-restore, #10). **This completes Item 5** (the customer delete-my-data workflow: locate → verify → two-person authorise → erase/minimise/retain → tombstone → notify processors → prevent restore). **HONEST SCOPE:** implementation + unit + integration + simulator-browser E2E are done; registering the REAL domain stores as erasable sources and the legal sign-off are external/deferred items for the Owner Action Register. **This is the technical workflow, NOT a claim of legal compliance.** `tests/e2e/erasure-console.e2e.ts` (1, real-browser; self-skips with no browser) |
| Customer "delete my data" — carrying the erasure out on the live surface, under the two-person control (Item 5 slice 5c, owner decision — DEVELOPMENT-APPROVED, LEGAL CONFIRMATION REQUIRED) (M20-FR-04 / PRV / DPDP, API-06, §28, P-04, P-08, hard rules #2 #6 #10) | `services/customer/src/erasure-execution.ts`, `services/api/src/adapters.ts`, `services/api/src/main.ts`, `services/api/src/roles.ts`, `tests/integration/erasure-execution.test.ts` | The engines (plan / executor / governance / processor-notice) were built and merged in 5a/5b; the M20-FR-04 executor was provider-neutral but **never wired to a route**. This slice makes the whole governed erasure reachable on the cloud, composing those engines and re-deciding nothing. **Locate PII:** `POST/GET /v1/privacy/pii/:customerRef[/:category]` records and reads, per customer, which categories of personal data the shop holds (count, statutory basis, minimisable) — the simulated, provider-neutral holding the executor acts on (event-sourced so the whole path is testable now, the "simulated sources" the executor was built for). **Prevent restore:** recording PII for an already-erased subject is refused via `guardAgainstRestore` — a late re-import cannot quietly bring a deleted person back (hard rule #10, P-08). **Maker-checker (SoD §28):** `POST …/erasure-approval` is a second, distinct officer's act (`privacy.erasure.approve`); `POST …/erasure-execution` is the maker's (`privacy.erasure.execute`), and `authoriseErasureExecution` refuses if the request is unverified (`not_verified`, 422), unapproved (`checker_missing`, 428) or approved by the same person who runs it (`maker_is_checker`, 409). **Execute → tombstone → notify:** on authorisation the route plans from the located PII, carries it out against the holdings (each held category an event-sourced erasable source; **retained categories are never touched** — hard rule #6), seals a **PII-free tombstone** (`GET …/tombstone`), and enqueues the provider-neutral processor notices on the durable connector queue; the request is only `fulfilled` when nothing was left partial, else honestly `partially_fulfilled` (P-08). Wired through the ordinary adapter/mount/roles path (`erasureExecutionAdapter` over a new `privacy` stream with pii/approvals/tombstones/processor-notices sub-streams; store-undefined fallback). **Proven end to end** against the real pipeline (`tests/integration/erasure-execution.test.ts`, 8): the full locate→verify→approve→execute→tombstone→notify path; retained invoice untouched; maker=checker / no-checker / unverified all refused; prevent-restore; RBAC (a cashier can neither record PII nor execute); durable across a cold restart; per-tenant. **HONEST SCOPE:** the governed workflow over a **simulated** located-PII holding — registering the REAL domain stores (orders, loyalty, profile) as erasable sources is the live-data-model step the executor's own header names, an external/deferred item for the Owner Action Register; the served DPO console + browser E2E are slice 5d. **This is the technical workflow, NOT a claim of legal compliance — the retention policy, the immutable-history boundary and the processor list need a lawyer's confirmation.** `tests/integration/erasure-execution.test.ts` (8) |
| Customer "delete my data" — telling the processors we shared the data with, provider-neutrally (Item 5 slice 5b, owner decision — DEVELOPMENT-APPROVED, LEGAL CONFIRMATION REQUIRED) (M20-FR-04 / PRV / DPDP, M32-FR-02, P-08, hard rules #6 #8 #10) | `packages/customer/src/processor-erasure-notice.ts`, `packages/customer/src/index.ts`, `tests/unit/customer-processor-erasure-notice.test.ts` | An erasure is not finished when the shop's own stores are cleared — the personal data it **shared** with processors/sub-processors (an SMS gateway, an email sender, a loyalty or analytics provider) must be erased there too, and a processor that is simply never told is the quiet gap that fails the person. This slice plans that notification, and does it **without inventing a second delivery mechanism**: the shop already has a tested, provider-neutral **connector queue** with bounded retry, throttling and a **read-never-deleted dead letter** (`packages/integration/src/connector.ts`, M32-FR-02). `planProcessorErasureNotices` takes the **tombstone** (what was erased / minimised) and the register of processors we shared each category with, and emits **one notice per processor that actually holds an affected category**, for **exactly that intersection** — a processor that shared only a legally-retained category is **not** notified (there is nothing to erase there, and telling it to erase a record the law makes us keep would be wrong). Each notice carries a provider-neutral `erase` instruction and a **stable key per (request, processor)**, so a re-plan or resend never doubles. The notices then ride the connector queue: a reachable processor is **delivered**, an unreachable one is retried and then **DEAD-LETTERED for a person — never lost** (hard rules #6 #8, P-08). Pure and deterministic (clock injected, nothing sent here). **Proven** in `tests/unit/customer-processor-erasure-notice.test.ts` (6): the intersection logic, the retained-only exclusion, idempotent keys, the neutral instruction, and — composing the real `drainConnector`/`deadLetters` — a reachable processor delivered while an unreachable one dead-letters and is surfaced on the queue. **HONEST SCOPE:** the planner + its unit/composition proof; registering the real processors and wiring the enqueue into the live erasure route is slice 5c. **This is the technical workflow, NOT a claim of legal compliance — the processor list and what each is told need a lawyer's confirmation.** `tests/unit/customer-processor-erasure-notice.test.ts` (6) |

A port that hands back the whole history obliges every implementation to read the whole history, so no adapter written against it could have been quick, and the cost was paid **on every sale**. The arithmetic is what makes it serious rather than untidy: SRE takes ~2,000 sales a day, which is 700,000 events in a year, so by month three each till was waiting on a scan of a quarter of a million rows to be told a two-word answer. It would not have shown up against a hundred fixtures, would not have shown up in the pilot's first week, and would have arrived as *"the tills have got slow"* with nothing obviously changed. The ports now **ask the question** — `isBanked(tenantId, saleId)`, `saleHoldingReceipt(tenantId, receiptNumber)`, `isKnown(tenantId, movementId)` — and the adapters answer each with one hit on `(tenant_id, idempotency_key)`, an index the store already had to carry because that uniqueness is what makes `append` idempotent. The tests are **ratios rather than absolute times**, so they mean the same thing on a laptop, in CI and on the shop's back-office PC, and one of them checks the **whole** intake read path rather than a single call, because one constant-time lookup next to a scan is still a scan. The harness takes the **best of three rounds** rather than one, which *tightens* the test: a round can only be made slower by something outside the code under test, so the fastest is the closest reading of the work itself. When one of these flaked under full-suite load, widening the ratio was the wrong repair for the reason the whole suite exists — a test loose enough never to flake is a test that cannot fail. The noise was real and the measurement was too small to see past it, so the answer was a better measurement. **And the same again for stock, where it is unbounded rather than merely large.** A hypermarket generates a few thousand movements a day — well over a million a year — and every availability lookup replayed all of them, which is somebody standing in an aisle or a customer watching a page. `project` now accepts an **opening balance** and the adapter folds from the last `InventorySnapshotTaken`, an event written on the *write* path (a handheld can afford an occasional extra fold; a lookup cannot) and keyed on the sequence it covers, so two writers racing produce one snapshot rather than two that disagree about where they start. **A snapshot is not a second source of truth**: it is derived from the ledger, it is itself append-only, and it can be deleted and rebuilt — an integration test proves a projection read *through* a snapshot equals a fold of the raw ledger, and the click-and-collect promise then reads through that same snapshot, so drift would surface as a wrong promise to a customer rather than as an abstract assertion. The first version of the snapshot work **passed its timing test while still reading every event and filtering to the tail in JavaScript** — correct, bounded in fold cost, unbounded in the read that actually reaches the database, and invisible on a stopwatch because filtering a million rows is quick compared with folding them. `readStream` gained `sinceSeq` and `type`, narrowed **at the store** (a range scan on `event_ledger_stream_idx`, and a binary search rather than a filter in the in-memory reference, since that is the store the edge runs on), and the guard for it **counts rows rather than milliseconds** — with a tripwire proving the counter does see a full read, so the assertion is not vacuous. **Two more of the same class, both in code written the same day.** *Today's takings* read every sale ever banked and then filtered to today — the one query in the system guaranteed to run against the largest table every morning, forever, because the owner looks at it daily; `readStream` gained a `from`/`to` window on `occurredAt`, served by `event_ledger_type_idx`, and the trading-day check stays *on top of* the window rather than replacing it, because the window is what makes the read cheap and the trading day is what makes it right when the shop trades past midnight (M09). And **consent was one stream for the whole shop**, so answering *"may we text this customer?"* — with somebody waiting at the counter — read every consent record the tenant held, a hundred thousand rows at twenty thousand loyalty customers; it is now **one stream per customer**, which is the shape the store's `(tenant_id, stream, seq)` index was built for — and the same correction was then applied across the surface: **a stream per driver-run** (settling one driver's Tuesday no longer reads every delivery the shop has ever made, and the two filters that used to do it are now the stream's name), **per location** for reservations, **per invoice** for purchase lines; while six reads that folded a whole stream to look at its last item — the AI kill switch, the budget cap, the enabled agents, the extraction operator — became one indexed row each. **The systematic guard is the one that will still be here for the fourteenth adapter**: it seeds a shop with twenty thousand events none of the reads care about, makes **every** adapter read, counts what came back, and names every one over budget **at once** — because one per run is several rounds of the same discovery. It found a case the individual tests had missed, and the finding was the **fixture**: it dated all ten thousand sales today, so the dashboard's per-day bound looked like no bound at all. A fixture that compresses a year into one day cannot show the difference between reading a day and reading a year, and the sales are now spread across days at the rate a shop actually trades. 12 assertions |
| The shop actually reaches the cloud (§31, §31.1, P-01, P-08, hard rules #1 #4 #6 #10) | `edge/sync-agent/src/http-transport.ts`, `tests/integration/the-shop-reaches-the-cloud.test.ts` | `SyncTransport` was a port with **no implementation** — "a thin adapter at deployment". Until now the edge committed sales durably before the receipt printed, queued them, reported its unsent count honestly, and had **nowhere to send them**. Every piece was tested apart; the join did not exist. **An event goes to the endpoint that would have handled it anyway**, and there is deliberately **no generic ingest**: a sale posted to `/v1/ingest` would skip the price check against the published pack, the receipt-number clash, the future-dated commit — the whole exception path — and land in the ledger having been examined by nothing, so a sale that syncs late goes through the same door as one that syncs immediately and gets the same answers. An event type with no route is **rejected by name** into the visible dead-letter queue (#6), not dropped and not posted somewhere hopeful. **The outcome mapping is the whole of the risk**, because `retryable` and `rejected` look almost identical in code and could not differ more in the shop: an unsent sale wrongly rejected stops being retried, and the money in the drawer has no cloud record until somebody works the queue. So a **timeout is retryable and is the common case** — a shop on a rural line meets it several times a day, and nothing about a slow link says the sale was bad; an **ambiguous outcome is retryable, never accepted**, because the receiver dedupes on the idempotency key so a duplicate delivery is one effect, whereas guessing \"accepted\" loses the sale silently and that is the one outcome with no way back; 5xx is retryable; a permanent 4xx is rejected so it cannot bury everything queued behind it; **408/425/429 are retryable** (4xx by number, transient by meaning); and **401 is retryable while 403 is rejected**, which is not the same question — an expired token is renewed by the next restart and the sale should still be waiting, while a permission the till does not hold will not appear by itself. The request carries **the event's own key**, minted when the sale was committed at the lane: a key minted per attempt makes every retry a new sale and the server doing everything right banks all of them. The token is never in a message and **the response body is never echoed**, because a body can quote the request and the request carries the header (#4) — asserted on every failure path, with a counter-test proving the token really is sent so the guard is about the messages rather than about its absence. The end-to-end gate drives the **real API surface against real PostgreSQL** with only the socket replaced: the shop trades five sales through an outage, nothing reaches the cloud and nothing is dead-lettered, the pass **stops early** rather than burning every item's attempt budget on a link that is plainly down, the badge tells the cashier the truth, the link returns and all five land — **once**, including when the edge restarted and lost its outbox and re-queued a sale it had already sent, which nothing at the edge can detect and only the cloud's dedupe can save. 15 unit + 9 integration assertions |

A driver id ending in something date-shaped, or a run date that ever gains a suffix, and two different runs compose to one stream — which means `reconcileRun` settles **cash, against a named person**, on the strength of a coincidence in string lengths. `packages/catalogue` learned the same lesson when joining fields with nothing let two products canonicalise identically. The parts are now joined with a **unit separator the data cannot contain**, and a part that somehow contains one is **refused rather than stripped**, because a stripped separator is a silently different stream — the failure this exists to prevent rather than a smaller version of it. Proved on the adversarial pair the hyphen collapses, on eight awkward driver/date combinations, and across all four kinds of stream, with a tripwire showing ordinary ids still compose. | The disk the receipt waits for (P-01, §31, NFR-03, hard rules #1 #2 #6) | `edge/store-edge/src/file-log.ts` | `DurableLog` was a port with a **test double behind it and nothing else** — `commitLocally`, the function that decides whether a receipt may print, was writing to an interface no deployment could satisfy, so the offline-first claim rested on a file that did not exist. **`fs.appendFile` returns when the bytes reach the operating system's cache, not the disk**, and on a back-office PC with no UPS the difference is a power cut between the receipt printing and the platters catching up: the sale is in the customer's hand and nowhere else. Every append is followed by an **`fsync`**, and `fdatasync` is deliberately *not* used — it skips metadata, and for an append the file's **length is metadata**, so the bytes can be on the disk under an inode that still says the file is shorter, which is the same lost sale by a subtler route. The **directory is synced once** at open, because a log that survived perfectly inside a directory that forgot its entry is not a log. Opened `'a'` (O_APPEND) — never `'w'`, which truncates — and the handle is **kept**, because opening per write puts an open, a sync and a close on the one path a customer stands and waits for. `usedBytes` comes from the filesystem rather than a counter, since a counter is right until the process restarts after a crash, which is exactly when the number decides whether the next sale is refused. **A truncated tail is quarantined by name, never parsed, never dropped and never repaired** (#6) — a repaired half-sale is a made-up sale — and truncation is decided by **arithmetic**: each record carries its byte length, so a short read is a calculation rather than a judgement about whether some JSON \"looks complete\". Found while writing it: the first framing escaped newlines so the file could be read with `split()`, which **corrupted every record containing the two characters backslash-`n` — exactly what `JSON.stringify` writes for a line break** — a lost sale produced by the code whose whole job is not losing sales. The length prefix makes escaping unnecessary and the reader now walks by offset. 11 assertions |
| The store edge starts, and trades, with no cloud at all (P-01, hard rule #1, §19, §31, P-08) | `edge/store-edge/src/main.ts`, `edge/store-edge/src/start.ts`, `infra/docker/edge.Dockerfile`, `infra/compose/docker-compose.yml` | Every piece of the edge existed and **none of it had ever been started**: no process, no durable log, no transport. A shop could not have run this. The property the whole file exists to demonstrate is **an absence**: with no `CLOUD_API_URL` and no `CLOUD_API_TOKEN` it opens its disk, reports itself ready to sell, and **says plainly that nothing will be synced** — it does not refuse to start, and it does not pretend. The compose service has **no `depends_on` and no required cloud setting**, so the stack can be brought up with the API stopped and the network unplugged and the shop still sells; if the edge needed the cloud to boot, offline-first would be a paragraph rather than a property, and the first power cut with a dead router would prove it in front of customers. `agent` is **null** rather than one pointed at nothing, which would fail a request every fifteen seconds forever. The sync loop is nowhere near the sale path: **passes cannot overlap** (the next is scheduled only after the last returns), the interval **backs off to a five-minute ceiling** so a shop with a dead router is not making a request a second all night and is not waiting hours once it returns, and a pass that throws is reported and the loop kept alive — a dead sync loop is a shop that silently stops syncing. **SIGTERM drains briefly and goes**: nothing is lost by stopping mid-drain, because an unacknowledged item stays pending, which is the whole reason there is an outbox. What a power cut left behind is **named on start-up**, not counted silently. The container **publishes no port** — the edge is not a service anybody calls, it owns a disk and drains a queue — runs non-root on a read-only root filesystem with its data on a named volume, and has **no health check that depends on the cloud**, because a shop whose line is down is trading perfectly well and a check saying otherwise gets the container restarted in the middle of a queue. 10 assertions |

Neither is a crash. Both are the control quietly not being there, which is the failure mode this repository spends most of its effort making impossible. Now SQL-backed, keyed `(tenant_id, key)`, with **`ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` and never an upsert** — the first answer under a key is the answer, because two requests racing under one key would otherwise leave the second's result stored against the first's hash and every later retry would be told about a request that never happened. The table is documented as a **cache and not a ledger**, and the distinction is load-bearing: expiring a row here is not deleting audit evidence (#6), because the event ledger holds what happened and is untouchable while this holds only what we answered — an expired key means a retry arriving days late is executed again, which is safe precisely because every append in the system is keyed and the ledger dedupes. A **tripwire proves the in-memory store forgets across instances**, so the rest is not merely proving that a database persists things. 6 assertions |

| A sale rung up at the lane reaches the cloud (P-01, §31, §31.1, hard rules #1 #6) | `edge/store-edge/src/index.ts`, `edge/store-edge/src/sync-cursor.ts`, `edge/store-edge/src/main.ts` | **The seam the whole product runs through, and it was not connected.** `createEdgeNode.commit()` wrote a sale to the disk and stopped: durable, correct, and **never queued** — so no sale a lane took ever reached the cloud. The enqueue now happens **after the durable write, never before**: queueing first would send a sale the lane went on to refuse, so the cloud would hold a sale that never happened and the customer walked away without paying for it — the same reasoning that prints the receipt second. **The outbox is rebuilt from the log on every start**, because the log is the system of record and the queue is a view of it; a queue that died with the process is not something to trust across a restart. It advances only over a **contiguous** prefix — a sale still pending, or one dead-lettered and now a person's problem, holds it where it is, because stepping over one means the next restart never re-queues it and that sale is gone with nothing saying so. | The receipt waits for the disk (hard rule #1, P-01, §31, M12) | `apps/pos/src/session.ts`, `apps/pos/src/view-adapter.ts`, `apps/pos/src/browser-entry.ts` | The seam one level above the last: `PosSession.commit()` priced, settled, appended to an **in-memory** ledger and queued to an **in-memory** outbox — all correctly, and none of it on a disk. Its own docstring said *\"commit the sale LOCALLY (hard rule #1)\"* and the function did not do it, **which is the most expensive kind of comment**: a lane that lost power between the sale and the next sync lost the sale, and the cashier had already seen \"Sale complete\". The durable write is now the **first** thing that happens — nothing is appended to the ledger, nothing is queued, and the state does not become `committed` until the sale is on the disk. `commit` is therefore **asynchronous**, and that is the point rather than a cost: the receipt number does not exist until the promise resolves, so there is nothing to print early with, and the guarantee is structural instead of a convention. The original *\"synchronous by construction — a sale never awaits the network\"* conflated two different things; **awaiting a local fsync is not awaiting the network**, and hard rule #1 asks for exactly that wait. A refusal is thrown as `LocalCommitRefusedError` carrying **the cashier's words rather than a code**, and it happens before the receipt exists, so nothing has been promised to anybody — the one place in the product where refusing a sale is the correct answer, correct because of the moment. The port is a **constructor argument and required**, not optional: an optional durable write is one a deployment can forget, and forgetting it is invisible, which is the exact shape of every other fault found today. The browser shell defaults it to a **refusal** rather than to acceptance, because a lane with nowhere to write must not take payment. Proved by recording the order of operations rather than assuming it — disk strictly before ledger and before outbox — and by a refused disk leaving the stock, the queue and the state all untouched. 5 assertions |

| The owner decides from a phone, on data that left the shop hours ago (M29, M29-FR-02, D13, M02, §28, §31, §31.1, QG-02, P-03, P-08) | `apps/owner-app/src/owner-session.ts`, `apps/owner-app/src/browser-entry.ts`, `apps/owner-app/web/`, `packages/approvals/src/reasons.ts`, `tests/unit/owner-session.test.ts`, `tests/unit/owner-app-boot.test.ts`, `tests/guardrails/the-owner-app-is-honest.test.ts` | `apps/owner-app/src/brief.ts` already built the day's numbers and the three things needing attention; what did not exist was anything that made them safe to **act** on. **The decision the file holds:** the owner is remote and every figure here is historical by construction — last-synced data, with the shop trading since it left. Reading the day on eleven-hour-old numbers is fine; approving a ₹8 lakh purchase order on them is not, and the difference between those two uses of one screen is the whole design. So a decision now **carries the ground it was made on**: `freshnessAtDecision` and `dataAgeSeconds` go into the decision itself, because *approved, on data eleven hours old, and he was told so* is a different fact from *approved* and only one of them can be defended later. On stale data the approve panel carries the age in words and the owner must act through it — **not a block**, because an owner who cannot approve while travelling telephones instructions instead and a telephoned approval has no audit trail at all. **One thing is blocked:** deciding when nothing has ever synced, since `missing` is not old data but *no* data and an acknowledgement of nothing is not informed consent. **The §31.1 case, built:** a decision made with no signal is queued, and while it waits the request can change or be withdrawn — so the queue is an **input** to the session (it outlives the app on a phone, and a queue lost silently is the worst way for an approval to disappear), and `reconcileQueued` compares each answer against the question as it now stands. A ₹40,000 approval that quietly applied to a ₹90,000 request is the exact failure maker-checker exists to prevent, so those come back to the owner: **never silently sent, never silently dropped.** The fingerprint that detects it is joined on a unit separator rather than concatenated, because a control that can collide is not one. **Three faults in the shipped shell, each invisible in review:** it answered a tapped alert with `window.alert('t-1\nt-2')` — a system dialog holding raw ids, a dead end wearing the clothes of an action; it rendered a fabricated ₹413 of takings **with no warning that they were sample figures**; and its language button set `document.documentElement.lang` and changed **not one word**, a toggle that says translated and is not. All three fixed and guarded. Every figure now drills to **every** sale behind it — never a sample, because a drill-through that disagrees with the figure it drills is only ever discovered by the person being asked to act. The decision vocabulary moved to `packages/approvals` so the manager's screen and the owner's phone write **one** vocabulary into one audit trail. **A repository-wide fault found on the way:** every guardrail had been scanning `*.bundle.js` build artifacts, so the suite passed or failed depending on whether somebody had run a build — the one thing a guardrail may never do. Excluded narrowly, with a test proving the hand-written shell beside it is still scanned. 50 unit + 32 guardrail assertions |
| The handheld and the driver's phone — and work that had nowhere to go (M19, M18, D09, §28, §31, §31.1, QG-02, P-01, P-08, hard rules #3 #6) | `apps/picker-app/src/pick-session.ts`, `apps/picker-app/src/browser-entry.ts`, `apps/picker-app/web/`, `apps/delivery-app/src/route-session.ts`, `apps/delivery-app/src/browser-entry.ts`, `apps/delivery-app/web/`, `packages/sync/src/device-outbox.ts`, `tests/unit/handheld-work-queues.test.ts`, `tests/guardrails/the-handheld-screens-are-usable.test.ts` | **The fault first, because it is the point.** Both session docstrings said the scans, the proof and the COD *"queue for sync afterwards"*. **Nothing queued.** Every resolved pick line and every completed stop lived in a JavaScript object on a device and nowhere else — the ninth and tenth instance in this project of a control that was described, believed and absent, and neither was caught by a single existing test. On the picker's handheld that loses an afternoon. On the driver's phone it loses **money that has already changed hands**: ₹6,000 collected across four stops, a dead battery, and no record anywhere that any of it was ever collected — the settlement has nothing to reconcile against, which is unfair to an honest driver and invisible for a dishonest one. The outbox is now a **required constructor argument** on both, because an optional port is one a deployment forgets and forgetting it is invisible; queueing happens in the single `replace()` each session funnels every state change through, so a path added later cannot skip it. `DeviceOutbox` writes through to the device after **every** mutation — enqueue, acknowledge, failure and dead-letter — because a decorator forwarding only `enqueue` would persist the work and lose the fact it had been sent, and the next boot would send all of it again; state and attempts are restored exactly, so a dead letter stays dead (hard rule #6). Restoration is a **constructor argument and nothing like it exists as a method** — an outbox whose contents can be rewritten after the fact is not evidence of anything. **Two model gaps the screens exposed.** `substitute` took `customerConfirmed: boolean`, and a boolean on a handheld is a tick box a picker with eleven lines left taps in half a second — true in the type system, unverifiable in the aisle. It now requires the customer's approval **reference**, which travels with the swap so a disputed substitution can be looked up rather than argued about; the screen scans it and has no free-text box at all. And the driver handed cash over with nothing counting it, so `handOver` now reconciles a **counted** figure against the recorded collections — **the blind count for the third time**, with no method returning the expected cash before a count, exactly as the till drawer and the stock count do it. **The screens:** no text input anywhere in the picker shell (the only way "every pick is a scan" survives a busy afternoon is if a crushed label cannot be typed around), global scan capture, a three-step indicator that actually advances — a guardrail caught the first version defining words for steps 2 and 3 and rendering only step 1, which is worse than no indicator because a picker told "step 1" while standing at step 3 stops reading it. Proof is asked for before money because that is the order it happens at a door; **card is not on the payment list at all**, so the engine's hard-rule-#3 refusal is one a driver can never walk into with a customer waiting; a failed delivery must say what happens to the goods next. What leaves either device is deliberately thin (§31): the order reference, the state, the money and the proof **kind** — never a customer name, never a phone number, and never the doorstep photograph, which would be a privacy problem being uploaded rather than a delivery being proved. 47 unit + 43 guardrail assertions |
| The warehouse handheld — receiving and put-away that decide on the served facts (M09, OA-9, §28, §31, §31.1, P-01, hard rules #1 #2 #10) | `apps/warehouse-app/src/warehouse-session.ts`, `apps/warehouse-app/src/browser-entry.ts`, `apps/warehouse-app/src/index.ts`, `tests/integration/warehouse-screen-fed.test.ts` | The owner's OA-9 decision is a dual-interface warehouse: a scanner-first offline PWA for the floor and a Web ERP supervisory surface, **both on the same authoritative services with no duplicated logic**. This is the first honest half of the PWA — the offline execution engine and the assignment feed it boots on — built **data-path first**, with the visual shell (bilingual strings, service worker, socket wiring) as the next work package. **The decision the file exists to hold: it orchestrates, it never re-decides.** Receiving is `packages/receiving`'s `receiveScan` unchanged — an unknown barcode goes to a resolution queue rather than becoming a closest match, a case is converted exactly or refused, a price edited at the door is refused (the three-way match depends on the agreed price), and an **over-delivery or a direct-store-delivery needs a SEPARATE approver** (§28: the approver can never be the receiver, checked on the payload the box served). Put-away and bin capacity are `packages/warehouse`'s `applyMovement`/`suggestPutAway` unchanged — an **unknown bin is queued for resolution, never invented** ("somewhere near aisle 4" is how stock becomes unfindable), a **full bin and an over-draw are refused** rather than going negative, and the item scanned must match what is waiting to be put away. Recall and expiry are `packages/fefo` — a recalled batch or an expired one is folded into the stock **state** so the one authoritative gate keeps it out of any pickable bin, and the worker is told **which** rule stopped them (recall vs expiry) rather than a generic refusal; the goods still go somewhere safe (a holding bin), because they are in the building either way (hard rule #10 — a refusal is a visible exception, not a silent drop). **Every accepted action queues for idempotent sync and a refusal queues nothing** (append-only, #2): a receipt queues `GoodsReceived`, a put-away queues `WarehouseMovementApplied` **keyed on the command id the cloud's movement ledger also keys on**, so a re-sent scan reconciles to one movement (hard rule #1 — commit locally first, sync idempotently). The outbox is a **required** constructor argument, exactly as on the picker handheld, because an optional queue is one a deployment forgets and forgetting it is invisible. Every scan returns a **feedback signal** — accept/warn/reject with a sound and a vibration length — so a rejected scan is felt as well as seen by someone in ear defenders in a cold store (OA-9 scan confirmation). A duplicate scan is a **warn**, not a reject, because it is a harmless no-op and the worker should not be told they did something wrong. 10 integration assertions |

So **every report is listed and an unavailable one is refused by name**, in the shop's own words — *nothing yet records what is thrown away* — which is the build backlog stated in business language. **The fault found inside the work, and the fifth instance of the session's recurring shape:** the first cut judged availability on the shop's records alone, so a tenant who started recording stock counts would have opened *Shrinkage*, satisfied every stated need, and been handed a page with no figures and no rows — under the report's real name, with a real as-at stamp on nothing, because the producer switch ended `default: return { figures: [], rows: [] }`. An empty shrinkage report reads as **no shrinkage**. A report is now runnable only when **both** halves hold — the shop records the facts AND this build computes them — `PRODUCED` names the second half, a test asserts it against the `case` labels in both directions, and the fallback **throws** rather than serving an empty dashboard. **The two gaps are told apart because they have different owners:** *nothing yet records that* is the owner's to fix and *this version cannot work it out yet* is ours, they carry different refusal codes, different words in both languages and a different colour, and a report we cannot build is kept off the owner's backlog entirely — he would do the work the screen asked for, open the report and find it blank. An empty backlog no longer reads as *every report works*. **Driven over the real socket, which found a second silent fault:** the payload had its own copy of the line-costing rule and divided by a thousand unconditionally — right for weighed goods, wrong for everything countable — so a ₹100 cost became 10 paise and the margin report read **99.92%**, the exact "a 100% margin is a lie that reads as very good news" failure arrived at from the other side. Nothing failed; the number was simply wrong. `lineCostMinor` and `basketUnits` are now exported from the read model and there is one implementation. **A bill with no readable lines** keeps its takings, which are real, and carries **no** basket size — a zero would be averaged into units-per-basket — and the count of those is reported beside the figure, as the margin already does for uncosted sales. **Nothing is written out under a name nobody holds:** an export's audit record is the only evidence afterwards of who took the shop's data, so the box serves the user the pack names and an absent one refuses the export outright rather than denying under a default id. **The comparisons of M29-FR-02 followed** once the day boundary existed to make them meaningful: *today against the last day we traded*, which **refuses when the box holds no earlier day** — a comparison against a day that is not there reports the shop as having doubled overnight against a nought nobody put in — and takes the previous day as the most recent *strictly earlier* one, so a future-dated sale from a lane with a wrong clock cannot become the thing today is measured against. The change is stated in **money rather than as a percentage**, because a percentage off a small day is a large number that means nothing on a screen people quote from. And *what is selling, by department*, in **units rather than money**: the log records a quantity per line but no money per line, so department revenue could only be rebuilt from list prices and a bill carrying a promotion would then produce a department total that does not add up to the day's takings — a figure that nearly reconciles is worse than one that is honestly a count. An item the catalogue places in no department is counted apart, never folded into one, because hiding it inside Grocery is how a catalogue problem stays invisible. 48 unit (session) + 13 unit (payload) + 17 integration + 41 guardrail assertions |

Every one of the eight already had a real producer beside it — `assessReconciliation`, `parallelRunPosition`, `outstandingExceptions`, the box's own outbox — and **`packages/migration/src/cutover-checklist.ts` is the join that was missing**, alongside fifteen more MG functions (`inventorySources`, `approveMapping`, `resolveException`, `signControlTotal`, `assessRetirement` and the rest) called by nothing outside their own tests: the largest instance of this codebase's recurring shape, and the one that matters most because of OB-06 — *the owner extracts his own data himself*, and a pipeline that can only be driven from a test file is a migration nobody can run. **NOT KNOWN FAILS:** every input is optional and every absence is a failure, never a comfortable default — no `?? 0` on the unsynced count, because "nobody told me" and "there are none" are opposite facts and only one is good news — and an **unanswerable** check is reported and drawn differently from one that came back **bad**, because a failed check is work to finish and an unanswerable one is a producer that was never connected. **A defect this screen introduced, found by driving it against a box mid-migration rather than reading it:** `sign` computed a signature, the view showed it green, and the next render re-read the payload and drew the total unsigned again — a signature that lived only in a browser tab. It is now **committed locally and queued** (hard rule #1, idempotency key `tenant:type:subject` so a replay collapses to one effect), the screen draws the working copy, and what has not reached the store computer is **counted on the page** (P-08). The person who ran the load can never sign its totals (§28) — and a box never told who ran it signs nothing at all; finance and tax totals are the CA's alone; a blocking exception is cleared by a decision including a decision to carry it, never by being unexamined, and is resolved and kept, never deleted (hard rule #6); the rollback is one clearly-labelled action needing nobody's approval, at any time, in any state, and retiring the legacy system never deletes the legacy data (MG-12). 21 unit (checklist) + 36 unit (session) + 11 integration + 32 guardrail assertions |
| Deployment (§19, §20, SEC-04/06, ADR-0002, hard rule #4) | `services/kernel/src/config.ts`, `services/kernel/src/http-server.ts`, `services/api/`, `infra/docker/api.Dockerfile`, `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | **A service with a missing or placeholder secret does not start.** It does not warn, substitute a default, or carry on reduced — a system that boots with a default signing key is a system running in production with one, and the log line saying so scrolled past three months ago. Everything is checked **at boot rather than on first use**, and **every problem is named at once**, because one per restart produces five deploys and a guessing game. The placeholder check reads the values that actually ship in `.env.example` — that file is what gets copied and forgotten — and a test reads the example file from disk so a newly added placeholder cannot slip past the refusal list. **Liveness and readiness answer different questions**: a database it cannot reach makes the API *not ready* and still *live*, because restarting will not reconnect a database and a crash loop buries the outage that caused it. **The store edge's required config contains no cloud setting at all** — if it needed the cloud to boot, offline-first would be a claim rather than a property (P-01). On SIGTERM the server **drains**: a request cut off mid-flight is a sale that reached the process and not the database while the till believes it was delivered. The container runs as a named non-root user, read-only root filesystem, no-new-privileges. CI **builds the image and proves the refusals**, expecting exit 78 (EX_CONFIG) and checking the message names every missing setting, then brings the whole stack to `/readyz`. Tested in `tests/integration/it-actually-starts.test.ts` — which boots on a real socket, since everything else in the suite is proved without one |
| The buyer's screen — and the eighty lines nobody has to retype (M06, M07-FR-04, M30-FR-01/03/04, D03, §28, A-03, QG-02, P-07, P-08) | `apps/web-erp/src/buying-session.ts`, `apps/web-erp/web/buying.html`, `apps/web-erp/web/buying.js`, `packages/purchasing/src/three-way-match.ts`, `edge/store-edge/src/screen-data.ts`, `tests/unit/erp-buying-session.test.ts`, `tests/guardrails/the-buying-screen-is-honest.test.ts`, `tests/integration/the-screens-are-fed.test.ts` | Every piece existed and was tested — `packages/purchasing` issues an order, `packages/import` validates a file and commits it atomically, `packages/receiving` books goods in, the three-way match pays the lowest of three — and **nothing captured a supplier invoice**, so `matchLines` returned an empty set for every one and the match refused every time, correctly and uselessly. Audit finding A-03 is somebody retyping an eighty-line invoice by hand every week, and this is the replacement. **The control that makes bulk capture safe rather than merely fast is the total printed on the paper.** The buyer types it off the bottom of the supplier's own document, and it is the only figure in the flow that does not come from the file — which is exactly why it can catch a line the file is *missing*, where every remaining line is perfect and nothing else in the system would notice. Proved end to end: a clean file short by one line previews with zero problems and is still refused. **Each line's own arithmetic is checked too** — quantity × unit price must equal the printed line total, reporting the source **line number** so somebody can go and look at the paper; the generic import engine validates types and references and has no idea what those three columns mean to each other. **Nothing writes before the preview and somebody else's approval**: the save button does not exist on the page until the model says the file may be saved (absent, not disabled — a disabled button is a thing to keep clicking), the commit is atomic because seventy-seven of eighty lines written is an invoice matching no piece of paper anywhere and nobody can say which three are missing, and a self-approval is refused (§28). **A real fault caught by its own test:** `match()` built its line set from the union of ordered ∪ received ∪ invoiced, so an invoice nobody had captured still produced rows with invoiced quantity zero and came back *not blocked* — the engine's own "an empty line set is not agreement" guard, defeated from the outside by handing it lines it should never have had. It now passes zero lines, and three documents cannot agree when we are holding two of them. **The buyer is stripped from their own approver list on the box**, not on the screen that would offer them, because separation of duties enforced only by the list somebody was shown is not enforced at all. **And what the box did NOT say is said**: every missing section here fails toward a refusal, which is the safe direction and still not honest on its own — "this was never ordered" looks identical whether the supplier invented the line or the box was never sent the order, and only one of those is an argument to have with a supplier, so each gap is named in a sentence on the page in both languages. The three-way match **moved from `services/purchase` into `packages/purchasing`** so the screen and the service run the same rule: a browser cannot import the HTTP kernel, and the alternative — a second copy of "what may we pay" — is one of them being wrong, found by a supplier paid one figure and reconciled against another. **The buyer's PO write-path now reaches head office (M06-FR-02, slice 1 toward E2E):** `createBuyingSession` exposes `canProposeToCloud` + `proposeToCloud`, which assemble `{ supplierId, lines[unitCost:Money] }` and PROPOSE the order through an injected `ProposePurchaseOrderPort` (destined for `POST /v1/purchase/orders/:poId` under the buyer's OWN session) — the cloud attributes the requisitioner to the authenticated caller and **no approver rides with the proposal**, so issuing stays a separate second-person §28 act the buyer cannot perform from this screen; a blocked supplier, an empty order or a dropped link is an honest `proposed:false` (P-08), never a false "raised", and an offline box with no port keeps its local compute (P-01). **Slice 2 wired the browser side:** `apps/web-erp/src/browser-entry.ts` `openProposePurchaseOrderPort` POSTs to `POST /v1/purchase/orders/:poId` (credentials same-origin, the PO id as the idempotency key so a re-click collapses to one order, a dropped link → `proposed:false`), and `buying.js`'s "Raise the order" button now calls `session.proposeToCloud` in the buyer's own name — the typed-name approver path is gone (`tests/unit/erp-buying-boot.test.ts`). **Slice 3 (M06 → E2E VERIFIED):** `tests/e2e/buying-po-delivery.e2e.ts` drives real headless Chromium against a stub cloud on one origin — both operator write-paths proven end to end: the PO-raise reaches head office (keyed by the PO id, no approver, a 422 shown and never a false raise, an empty order refused before any POST) AND the invoice capture (A-03) commits atomically with a second person's approval, offline-first with no network call, the buyer refused their own approval (§28). 31 buying-session unit + 10 buying-boot unit + 5 browser-e2e + 12 integration + 27 guardrail assertions |

## Assembly state — what "Built" above does and does not mean

The family table certifies **domain logic and its tests**. It does not certify a system anybody can
switch on, and reading it alone would leave that impression. Measured, not estimated:

| Layer | Source | State |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| `packages/` — domain logic | ~44,800 lines, 247 files | **Complete.** Every module M01–M36, 2,673 tests |
| `apps/pos` | ~990 lines + PWA shell, service worker, manifest | **Runnable shell.** Lane guards, session, view adapter, offline cache |
| `apps/web-erp` | ~5,700 lines + **eleven** PWA shells (767-line manager view, 580-line buyer view, 700-line product/price view, 560-line shelves/space view, 394-line reporting view, 430-line service-desk view, 380-line expiry/recall view, 400-line finance view, 380-line admin/security view, 420-line AI-control view, 480-line migration view), service worker, manifest | **Runnable shell.** Approvals inbox, receiving, blind count, day close by exception; the buyer's screen (supplier-invoice capture against the printed control total, the three-way match, raising an order); the product and price screen (completeness scoring, publish, recall block, an effective-dated price change against the MRP ceiling and the margin floor, price history, promotion simulation); the merchandising and space screen (blind shelf counts, refill tasks that never fire on an uncounted facing, the range review, what each part of the floor earns per square foot); the reporting screen (every report D13 names, the ones this shop cannot run listed as prominently as the ones it can and saying which of the two gaps it is, and an audited export); **and the service desk** — receipt lookup from the box's own log, the at-most-once return guard fed at last, refunds that never claim a card has been repaid, and complaints with their SLA clock and compensation under maker-checker. **and expiry and recall** — the action list, FEFO, and a recall that reports what is still in customers' homes and will not close without evidence. **and finance** — both sides of every control total, the Tally queue beside them and never inside them, and a month that closes only when every figure agrees. **and admin and security** — outside access that is scoped, time-bound and judged live from the clock; who can get in; the fleet; and what the retention rules would do. **and AI control** — a kill switch that now actually stops a model call, what each assistant may do and what no assistant may ever do, everything it has drafted waiting for a named person, and what it has cost against the owner's own ceiling. **and migration** — the eight-check cutover gate DERIVED from the real state rather than ticked by hand, the figures signed by somebody who did not load them, the old data's problems kept and decided, and a rollback that needs nobody's approval. One bundle, eleven pages, because these are eleven jobs for eleven people (P-07) |

**The consequence, stated plainly so it cannot be missed (reconciled 7 Aug 2026 against the audit):**
the business rules are finished and the system is **only partially assembled**. An earlier version of
this paragraph said "there is no service layer" — that is now **stale**: a thin service layer exists
and all thirteen APIs persist to PostgreSQL (see the table above). But two facts qualify every
"Built" below and must be read with it:

1. **The services are still thinning out — but measurably less thin.** Early on, six of the seven
   domain services were kernel-only re-implementations that did **not** import the rich tested engines
   in `packages/`. The **CORE-01…05** wiring workstream has been collapsing that gap one reviewed
   increment at a time — fulfilment, ai, reporting, finance (credit-notes, notes), stored-value/loyalty,
   returns, purchase, and now **compliance** all run their `packages/` engine on the live API.
   **5 of 79 packages are now imported only by their own tests** (down from 35) — and the CORE-05
   wiring workstream is **COMPLETE**: **every genuine domain engine is now on the live API.** The five
   that remain are shared libraries or frontend that by design do not sit behind a service route
   (`types`, `utils`, `config`, `ui`, `api-client`) — a type package or a UI-component package has no
   endpoint to serve. The ten engines wired across CORE-05 were `compliance`, `quality`, `self-checkout`,
   `owner-control`, `reversal`, `notifications`, `ops`, `org`, `documents` and `suspended-sales`.
   (`packages/e-invoice` and `packages/restricted-sales` are new packages, each added and wired in the
   same increment — for A20 e-invoicing and B14 tobacco restrictions — never test-only, so the total is
   now 79 packages with the same 5 unwired-by-design.)
2. **"Built" ≠ end-to-end.** A requirement row reading *Built* means its rules are implemented and
   unit-proved. It does **not** mean a cashier can scan an item today, nor that the row is
   *WIRED / INTEGRATION TESTED / E2E VERIFIED* in the sense of the completion vocabulary below.

The ASSEMBLY / WIRING workstream (below) tracks each module through that vocabulary. This section is
the honest counterpart to the family table above and must be read beside it.

## Completion status vocabulary (adopted 7 August 2026)

Per owner instruction, "engine implemented and unit-tested" is **not** "module complete." Every module
is now tracked through this ladder; a module is COMPLETE only when the whole chain — requirement →
domain engine → application/service → API/event contract → persistence → authorization → UI/channel
where applicable → integration tests → E2E → operational evidence — is connected and verified.

`NOT STARTED` · `ENGINE ONLY` · `PARTIALLY WIRED` · `WIRED` · `INTEGRATION TESTED` · `E2E VERIFIED` ·
`UAT VERIFIED` · `PRODUCTION VERIFIED` · `EXTERNALLY BLOCKED`

Never report `ENGINE ONLY`, simulated, synthetic, mocked, or documented work as product completion.
The evidence each rung requires is the mandatory **`docs/MODULE-COMPLETION-TEMPLATE.md`**, copied into
every module-assembly PR; a module moves up only to the highest rung whose boxes are ticked. This is
**CI-enforced**: `tests/guardrails/completion-ladder-has-evidence.test.ts` fails the build if any
module below claims `WIRED`+ without registered evidence that exists (and `INTEGRATION TESTED`+ must
point at a real integration/e2e test), so an engine-only module cannot be labelled complete. The
shared E2E harness (`tests/support/api-harness.ts`) and local/test IdP (`tests/support/local-idp.ts`)
are how `E2E VERIFIED` is proved — through the real surface, real token verifier and real per-tenant
authorization, the way `main()` composes them.

## Store audit findings F01–F17 (independent store-workflow audit, 30 September 2026, commit 8f4f6c5; F13–F15 from SP-9-i's connected run, F16 from SP-9-ii's and F17 from SP-9b-i's, 1 October 2026)

The owner commissioned an independent audit of the core store chain (handover package *Hyper-Market-Store-E2E-Handover*,
pinned to `8f4f6c5a62cffda0bae838cc7fde1196cf8135e3` = current `main`). Its twelve reproduced findings are registered
HERE, against the requirements they belong to, so the canonical record carries them; the dated owner view is
`docs/audit/STORE-E2E-STATUS-MATRIX-2026-09-30.md`. The audit's observation tests are committed under
`tests/audit-observations/` **as defect reproductions — a pass confirms the defect**; F13–F17 were found by the connected runs on the real stack (SP-9-i, SP-9-ii and SP-9b-i, 1 Oct 2026) and are registered the same way; the slice that fixes a finding
inverts its assertion into the intended-behaviour regression (never restores the bug to keep a test green). No module
rung or score changes with this registration: a rung records what the evidence shows, and every finding below is a
missing JOIN or a missing GUARD, not a missing engine. **Status legend:** OPEN (reproduced at the commit named) ·
FIXED (PR named, regression inverted).

| F01 | A committed partial GRN changes stock but leaves the approved PO fully outstanding — the receipt fold into the PO commitment is a separate call nobody makes — **FIXED in SP-6, 30 Sep 2026:** a goods receipt against an ISSUED purchase order folds into the order in the SAME atomic `appendBatch` as the GRN and its stock movements: `receivedAgainstOrder` / `poPostingFor` on `services/inventory/src/goods-receipt.ts` post the received quantity per product (sellable + quarantined — what came into our custody; never the held excess until a second person accepts it, never what was refused at the dock) as a `PurchaseOrderReceiptPosted` on the purchase-order stream keyed on the GRN id (`poReceiptEvent` in `services/api/src/adapters.ts`), so `computeOpenCommitment` nets it exactly as a manual posting and a retried GRN folds nothing twice; an accepted held excess posts `<grnId>:excess` in the excess decision's own append (the over-receipt shows as a negative open quantity, a signal). The ORDERED quantity on each line is the order's, never the body's (`alignToOrder`; `ordered_quantity_disagrees` / `product_not_on_order` said, F07). A receipt with no order, an unknown order, or an order not yet issued is received and flagged (`no_purchase_order` / `order_unknown` / `order_not_issued`) and folds into nothing. Direct and relayed (manager screen) routes take the same path (`orderForReceipt`). The manual `POST /v1/purchase/orders/:poId/receipts` remains for receipts recorded outside the GRN path and collapses with the GRN when it uses the GRN id.
